## Not one road

The term "Seidenstraße" was coined by Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877. Nobody at the time called it that, and it was never a single road. Valerie Hansen, *The Silk Road: A New History* (OUP, 2012), p. 235, is blunt: most trade was local, carried short distances by people who never saw the far end. The romantic image of caravans crossing from Chang'an to Rome is mostly wrong, and I have to unteach it every year.

## The Sogdians

The real middlemen. Iranian-speaking merchants based around Samarkand and Bukhara, with communities strung out across China. The Sogdian Ancient Letters, found by Aurel Stein in a watchtower near Dunhuang in 1907, date to around 313 AD. Letter 2 is from a merchant reporting the sack of Luoyang. Letter 3 is from a woman, Miwnay, abandoned in Dunhuang by her husband, telling him she would rather have married a dog or a pig. Students remember Miwnay.

## Dunhuang and the Library Cave

Sealed some time around 1000 AD, found in 1900 by the Daoist monk Wang Yuanlu. Stein took thousands of manuscripts in 1907, including the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book (block-printed, see [[Printing press]]). It's in the British Library, Or.8210/P.2. The Chinese view of Stein is not the British one, and that's worth an entire lesson.

## What actually moved

- Silk, yes, but also paper, which moved west after the battle of Talas in 751 (that story is probably too neat).
- Religions: Buddhism east, later Islam, Nestorian Christianity, Manichaeism.
- Glass from the Mediterranean; one Roman-style glass bowl ended up in the Shōsōin in Nara, which I want to see after [[Kyoto]].
- Disease, eventually. The plague of 1346 rode the same routes.
- Later, coffee came the other way to Istanbul, see [[Ottoman coffeehouses]].

## For class

Map exercise SR-2Y-04: give them the Tang frontier and the passes, let them plan a route and cost it in bolts of silk (the Tang army paid soldiers in silk). Then show them the [[长城修建]] map and ask why the wall and the trade routes run the way they do.
